format:
A deck is YAML: {deck: {title, lang (zh-TW|en|...), voice?, speed? 0.5-2 = speaking speed, 1.5 = 1.5x faster (set it when the user asks for a faster/slower voice)}, chapters: [{title, slides: [slide...]}]}.
slide: {id?, layout?, title, subtitle? (title slides), bullets? [<=6 short strings], narration? (what is SPOKEN; also the subtitles),
visual?, cues? [..], transition? {type, ms}, duration? (seconds; only for silent slides), notes? (speaker notes, PPTX only)}.
layout (optional, inferred): title (opening slide: title + subtitle), topic (a big chapter-divider title), content (bullets),
split (bullets left + visual right), visual (the visual fills the slide). Slide 1 is normally a title slide; start each chapter
with a topic slide only when the chapter is long.
transition.type: fade (default) | slide-left | slide-right | push | zoom | wipe | curtain | spin | fly | none; ms 100-3000 (default 500; 1400
between 3D slides). It describes how THIS slide enters. Vary them a little; use one style for slides in the same chapter and a different
one at a chapter start. Between 3D slides fly (the camera flies to the next slide's shot; the default there) is the native one, spin
(the model turns away and the next one turns in) also works, and curtain only closes real curtains in the opera environment;
fade works everywhere.
3D: deck.style: flat (default) | 3d sets the look of every slide, slide.stage overrides it for one slide, so flat and 3D slides can be
mixed in one deck. deck.environment (3d only): template (default: follows the company slide template -- light floor on the white page, navy behind title
slides) | studio (dark) | opera (a theatre with curtains and spotlights, only if the user asks) | space.
Read get_presentation_topic("3d") before using 3D.
Sizes: <=150 slides, <=30 chapters, narration <=1200 characters, bullets <=220 characters, one deck plays for at most ~75 minutes
(counted with the speaking speed). A long talk (30 minutes = 50-70 slides) is still ONE deck: write it chapter by chapter with
begin_presentation / add_chapters / finish_presentation instead of one huge render_presentation call.
layout:
Picking a layout: opening -> title. Chapter start -> topic (title only, short narration) or fold the chapter name into the
first content slide. A list of points -> content (<=4 bullets is best; the viewer reveals them one by one with the narration).
Points + a picture/diagram/table -> split (bullets stay short: the visual carries the detail). A big diagram, a wide table or
a screenshot -> visual. Last slide: a summary/next-steps content slide.
Rhythm: 25-40 seconds of narration per slide (~2-5 short sentences, about 60-180 CJK characters); a 5-minute talk is ~8-12 slides.
visuals:
visual: {kind, mode? (loop|timed, default loop), period? (seconds of one loop), motion? (none|float|pulse|spin|kenburns), ...}
Every visual is ALWAYS in motion or revealed over time (this is an animated slide, never a dead picture):
  shapes   {scene: {width, height, duration, background, shapes: [...]}} -- the same format as a 2D animation: circle/rect/polygon/
           line/text/image shapes, each with an optional "id" and an "animation" (move/rotate/scale/fade/orbit/keyframes). Best for
           explanatory diagrams you draw yourself (flows, layers, a signal moving along a path). Give shapes ids and reveal them
           with cues (show: "shape:<id>"). Call get_2d_animation_topic-style details from the 2D animation vocabulary: "position":[x,y],
           circle "radius", rect "width"/"height", line/polygon "points":[[x,y],...], text "content"/"font_size", "fill", "stroke",
           "stroke_width", animation {type: move, from:[x,y], to:[x,y], duration:s, loop: true|pingpong} {type: rotate, speed: deg/s}
           {type: orbit, center:[x,y]|parent:id, radius, speed} {type: scale, min, max, speed} {type: fade, from, to, duration, loop}
           {type: keyframes, keyframes:[{t, position, rotation, scale, opacity}]}.
  mermaid  {source: "flowchart LR; A[Start]-->B[Next]"} -- flowcharts, sequence, state, class diagrams. Drawn once, gently floating; reveal with cue
           show: visual. Keep labels short (<= 12 characters). Put every label that has a / \ ( ) or other
           punctuation in double quotes: A["/help"] --> B["設定 (選填)"] (a bare [/help] is read as a shape and fails).
  svg      {svg: "<svg viewBox=...>...</svg>"} inline markup (no scripts) or {src: url of an .svg}.
  chart    {src: url returned by render_chart}.
  table    {header: [..], rows: [[..],..]} (<=8 columns, <=12 rows, cells <=120 characters). Rows appear one by one (or cue "row:N").
           Long tables: split over several slides ("... (1/2)", "... (2/2)"), or keep the 3-5 rows that matter and say so in the narration.
  image    {src: "@img3"} or {images: [{src, caption}], fit?: contain|cover, callouts?: [{x,y,w,h (fractions 0..1 of the picture), text}]}
           -- a real picture from a source (see "sources"). Several images take turns every <period> seconds (a slideshow), or use
           cue show: "image:N". callouts draw an orange box (+label) on the picture and appear with cue show: "callout:N" -- use them
           to point at the part of a screenshot the narration is talking about. motion kenburns = a slow zoom.
  anim2d   {ref: "client-file/<file_id>" of an uploaded .2danim.yaml}. (Normally draw with kind shapes instead.)
  scene3d  a LIVE 3D model animation: {scene: {nodes: [...]} inline (vocabulary: get_3d_scene_topic), or ref: "client-file/<file_id>" of an uploaded .3dscene.yaml,
           interactive?: true, orbit?: seconds}. The viewer can drag to orbit and wheel to zoom it. See get_presentation_topic("3d").
  group    several visuals side by side in one slide: {items: [{box: [x, y, w, h] (fractions 0..1 of the visual area), kind: ..., ...}, ...]}
           -- up to 4, e.g. a 3D model next to a table, or a screenshot next to a flowchart. Cues bullet:/row:/callout:/image:/shape: address
           the first element of that kind in the slide.
  code     {code: "<the text>" | src: url of a text attachment, lang?: c|python|js|bash|json|yaml|sql|diff..., filename?, patch?: true|false,
           size?: 14..44, start_line?, highlight?: [12, [20,25]], autoscroll?: true|seconds} -- a LONG listing or a patch/diff in a
           scrollable window with line numbers, syntax highlighting and a scrollbar (the viewer scrolls it; MP4 shows it scrolling by itself
           when autoscroll is on; PPTX gets a picture of the current view). A git patch / unified diff is recognised by itself (green/red
           lines, hunk headers, each file highlighted in its own language). USE THIS whenever the material is code, a log or a patch longer
           than ~12 lines: do not cut it into bullets or screenshots. Give the text with define_snippet(kind: "code", content: ...) and write code: "@c1" (a patch: define_snippet(kind: "patch") -> code: "@p1"; no yaml escaping). Put the part you talk about on screen with start_line / highlight.
  terminal {commands?: ["ls", "echo hi"], title?, interactive?: true|false} -- a REAL shell (busybox ash in the browser) in the slide:
           the commands are typed and run when the slide is first shown, then the viewer can type. MP4 / PPTX show its current screen.
           The deck WAITS at the end of the slide until the viewer has typed a command (they were asked to): for a terminal that only
           demonstrates (nobody types) set wait: false, or interactive: false. Ask in the narration what to type.
  quiz     an interactive answer card (Q&A, scored): see get_presentation_topic("interactive").
  widget   YOUR OWN interactive piece (a game, a simulator, a drag-and-drop exercise) as one HTML document in a sandbox:
           see get_presentation_topic("interactive").
  overlay  on ANY visual (also on a 3D model): overlay: {scene: {width, height, shapes: [...]}} -- a 2D layer (same shapes format as kind
           "shapes") drawn over it: labels, arrows, circles and highlights that appear with cues (show: "shape:<id>"). This is how 2D annotation
           is mixed with 3D.
3d:
2D and 3D mix in the SAME format; 3D is a look you give a slide, not a different kind of deck.
- A 3D model: visual {kind: scene3d, scene: {duration, background, camera, nodes: [...]}} written inline (call get_3d_scene_topic for
  the vocabulary; it is a declarative node list: box/sphere/cylinder/cone/torus/polygon/particles..., each with
  position, material and an animation spin/bounce/orbit), or ref: "client-file/<file_id>" of an uploaded .3dscene.yaml. Keep it to ~5-25 nodes. It animates with the slide clock and the viewer can
  drag to orbit / wheel to zoom it.
- A 3D SLIDE: deck.style: 3d (all slides) or stage: 3d on single slides, with a scene3d visual. The slide is the SAME company-template page as a flat
  slide (title, chapter label, green-dot bullets, subtitle bar); the model is shown in a VIEWPORT (a rounded window) where a flat slide has
  its visual, and the slide's CAMERA looks into the 3D scene through it. The slide says where the camera is:
    camera: front | three-quarter (default) | left | right | back | top | wide | closeup        one shot, by name
    camera: {preset?, azimuth: -360..360 (deg, 0 = in front, + = to its right), elevation: 0..89 (deg), distance: 0.1..6 (x the distance that
             frames the whole model; < 1 closer), focus: <id of a node of the model>, fov: 20..80, at?: "sentence:N" | "sec:S"}
    camera: [shot, shot, ...]    up to 8 shots: the camera moves (about 1.2 s, eased) from one to the next while the narration goes on; a
             shot with at: starts then, the others share the narration evenly, the first starts the slide.
  The relation between camera and model is the point of a 3D slide: name the part you are talking about (focus: <node id>, e.g. the id of
  the fan node in the scene you made) and put it in the shot at the sentence that mentions it (at: "sentence:2"); show the whole thing
  first (wide / three-quarter), then close in (closeup + focus), then pull back for the next idea. closeup without a focus just comes closer.
  Between two 3D slides the camera flies (transition fly). The viewer can still drag / wheel on top of the shot; it snaps back when the slide
  changes. Title / topic slides with a model are full-bleed 3D on the template's navy.
  Everything else keeps working in a 3D slide (title, bullets, subtitles, tables, images, 2D shapes, group items are drawn flat):
    a 3D slide:   {stage: 3d, title, bullets (short: the viewport is on the right), visual: {kind: scene3d, scene: {...}}, camera, narration, cues}
    3D + 2D:      visual: {kind: scene3d, scene: {...}, overlay: {scene: {width: 977, height: 690, shapes: [{id: tag1, type: text, content: "CPU", position: [480, 300], ...}]}}}
                  with cues [{at: "sentence:2", show: "shape:tag1"}] -- 2D labels that appear over the viewport (the overlay is fixed to the
                  window, it does not follow the 3D part when the camera moves; keep overlay labels for shots that stay still).
    side by side: visual: {kind: group, items: [{box: [0.0, 0, 0.6, 1], kind: scene3d, scene: {...}}, {box: [0.62, 0.1, 0.38, 0.8], kind: table, header, rows}]}
                  (the 3D item's box is the viewport; the other items are flat panels at their boxes).
- In a flat slide (no stage) a scene3d visual is a live 3D view inside the usual visual area, slowly orbiting (orbit: false stops it).
- Choose 3D when the subject IS a thing in space (hardware, a board, a mechanism, a topology, an architecture as blocks) -- not for
  text-only slides. A deck can open flat, show 3D slides for the physical parts and return to flat for tables and summaries.
- Without WebGL (or when the 3D view cannot start) a deck still plays: 3D slides fall back to the flat look and a 3D model is drawn by a
  software renderer.
cues:
cues sync the picture with the narration: [{at: "sentence:N" | "sec:S", show|emphasize: TARGET, effect?: fade|rise|pop|wipe|pulse, ms?}].
at: sentence:N is the START of the Nth sentence of the narration (1-based; sentences end at 。！？.!?；). TARGET: title | visual | bullet:N
(0-based) | row:N | callout:N | image:N | shape:<id>. "show" makes the element appear at that moment (hidden before); "emphasize"
pulses an element that is already there.
Bullets with no cue are revealed one per sentence automatically (skipping an introductory first sentence), table rows one after
another -- write cues only when you want something else. Write the narration so that its sentences line up with what appears:
sentence 1 introduces, sentence 2 -> bullet 0, sentence 3 -> bullet 1 ...
interactive:
Interactive pieces: the viewer DOES something on the slide. Three kinds -- all work with narration, cues and layouts like any visual,
and in PPTX / MP4 they turn into static text / a picture (the PPTX gets the question, "你的回答" and "我們回應:" when the viewer answered).

THE WHOLE DECK HAS THIS SHAPE (copy it; a deck with slides at the top level, or without deck: and chapters:, is refused):
  deck: {title: 互動示範, lang: zh-TW, speed: 1.2}
  chapters:
    - title: 內容
      slides:
        - title: 開場
          narration: 一到三句短句。
        - title: 這一頁的重點
          narration: 旁白。
          visual: {kind: code, lang: c, code: "@c1"}
Leave out layout, cues and transition unless you need them (a transition is a mapping {type: fade, ms: 500}, never a bare word; types:
fade slide-left slide-right push zoom wipe curtain spin fly none). Fewer fields = fewer errors.

1) quiz -- an answer card with a score.
  {kind: quiz, type: choice|multi|short|open|terminal, question, options?: [2-6], answer?, accept?: [..], explain?, points?: 10,
   grading?: static|ai, reference?, rubric?, check?, terminal?, wait?: true}
  - choice: options + answer: 1 (0-based index or the option text). multi: answer: [0, 2] (partial credit, wrong picks subtract).
  - short: answer: "text" (also accept: ["alt", "/regex/i"]); typed answers match ignoring case, spaces and punctuation.
  - open: free text, graded by an AI against reference (the model answer) and rubric (what earns points).
  - terminal: a task done in a real shell inside the card: terminal: {commands: [setup lines]}, check: {output: "/regex over the screen/",
    cmd: "/regex over what was typed/"} (each check is an equal share of the points), or grading: ai.
  - grading: static (default when there is an answer key: instant, offline) | ai (default for open; a model scores 0..1 with feedback).
  - explain: shown after grading. An answer card always makes the deck WAIT at the end of its slide until the viewer submits (or pages on with ›); wait: false lets the deck run past it. A widget does not wait unless you set wait: true.
  One card per slide (or one item of a group). Put the question on the slide, ask it in the narration, and say what happens next.
  THE VIEWER MUST SEE WHAT THE QUESTION IS ABOUT. A question about code, a patch, a log, a diagram or a table is put on the SAME slide as
  that material -- never "in the patch above" on a slide that shows only the options. Use a group: code (or image/table) on the left, the
  card on the right, e.g.
    visual: {kind: group, items: [{box: [0, 0, 0.56, 1], kind: code, patch: true, code: "..."},
                                   {box: [0.58, 0, 0.42, 1], kind: quiz, question: "...", options: [...], answer: 1}]}
  (quote only the few lines the question needs, so the card stays readable.) A card alone on a slide gets the whole area.
  The wrong options of a code / patch question must differ CLEARLY from the right one -- never the same line with one identifier changed
  ("Node *new = f(v);" vs "Node *new_node = f(v);" confuses everybody: if the patch renames it, ask about something else), and never a line the
  patch also adds or changes somewhere else. A patch with an identical line removed and added is refused.
  Write questions with exactly ONE right answer that can be worked out from what is on screen, and make `explain` agree with `answer`
  (re-read both before you finish: the answer index is 0-based, the first option is 0). For "which line was added?" make exactly one option
  an added line and the others unchanged or removed lines.
  A patch you write (kind code) must be a real unified diff: "diff --git a/f b/f", "--- a/f", "+++ b/f", hunk headers "@@ -12,6 +12,8 @@",
  context lines start with ONE SPACE, removed lines with "-", added lines with "+". Never remove and re-add the identical line.
  A quiz deck: 1 explanation slide, then 1 card slide, repeat; end with a summary slide (the viewer sees the running score in the player).

2) terminal -- {kind: terminal, commands: [...]} a real shell the viewer can type into (see "visuals").

3) widget -- you write the interactive piece yourself, like making a small game.
  FIRST call define_snippet(kind: "widget", content: <the full html>) -- the html is its own tool argument, NOT inside the yaml (a game
  inside a yaml string means escaping every quote and backslash twice, and it fails again and again). It checks the html at once and
  returns a handle "@w1". THEN in the deck yaml:
  {kind: widget, html: "@w1", fallback: "what it is and what the viewer does (1-3 sentences)",
   title?, points?: 100, wait?: false, start?: countdown|click|auto, grade?: {question, reference|rubric}}
  START: the viewer sees a "點一下開始" button first (over the card that shows your fallback text), clicks, a 3-2-1 countdown runs, and only
  THEN is your html loaded -- so the game's clock and first frame start at that moment (start: click = no countdown, auto = at once). Do not
  write your own start screen or timer for this; just start the game when your script runs.
  THE CAGE: the html runs in a sandboxed iframe. NO network (no fetch / XMLHttpRequest / WebSocket, no <script src>, no <link>, no http(s)
  url, no @import), no localStorage / cookies / parent page, no nested frames. Everything is inline: <style>, <script>, <canvas>/SVG/DOM;
  images only as data: uris (or draw with canvas). Max 120000 characters. The validator refuses anything else and tells you which.
  Fill the iframe: use width/height 100% (canvas sized from window.innerWidth/innerHeight, redraw on resize). Support mouse AND touch
  AND keyboard (arrow keys, space) because the viewer may use any. Give a visible score and a restart button. The page is white by
  default; style it (dark game backgrounds are fine). Text in the viewer's language (deck.lang).
  THE BRIDGE: a global `deck` exists:
    deck.points          the points the widget is worth (the slide's "points", default 10) -- the score it can reach
    deck.score(got, max?, feedback?)  report the CURRENT score (0..points; if max is given it is rescaled to points); call it every
                         time the score changes, not only at the end. Reaching `points` counts as a win.
    deck.done()          the viewer finished (won, lost or gave up)
    deck.summary(text)   one line shown on the slide card / in PPTX ("通關!用了 42 秒")
    deck.save(obj) / deck.onInit(function(saved){...})   keep a small JSON state (restored when the pack is opened again)
    deck.grade(answerText) -> Promise<{score 0..1, feedback}>  ask the AI grader to judge free text (needs the "grade" setting;
                         at most 20 per widget) -- for exercises like "explain this in your own words" inside your own UI.
  Ideas: a game that must reach N points to win (breakout / space shooter / invaders; each hit scores a random 5-15), a sorting or
  matching game, a circuit / state-machine simulator the viewer pokes, a timeline to drag events into order, a parameter slider that
  shows a result live, a flash-card round. Make it tied to the talk's subject, playable in 30-90 seconds, forgiving (no instant
  game over without a restart button).
  Example -- "win 100 points at breakout, each brick gives a random 5-15" (compact; adapt, do not shrink the feedback and restart).
  Step 1, define_snippet(kind: "widget", content: the html between the two marker lines):
  --- widget html begin ---
    <canvas id=c style="display:block;width:100%;height:100%;background:#0b1626"></canvas>
    <script>
    var c=document.getElementById('c'),x=c.getContext('2d'),W,H,pad,ball,bricks,score,over;
    function reset(){W=c.width=innerWidth;H=c.height=innerHeight;pad={x:W/2,w:W*0.18,y:H-30};
      ball={x:W/2,y:H-60,vx:3.2,vy:-4.2,r:8};bricks=[];score=0;over=false;var cols=8,rows=5,bw=W/cols;
      for(var i=0;i<cols;i++)for(var j=0;j<rows;j++)bricks.push({x:i*bw+2,y:50+j*26,w:bw-4,h:22,alive:true,pts:5+Math.floor(Math.random()*11)});
      deck.score(0);}
    function step(){if(!over){ball.x+=ball.vx;ball.y+=ball.vy;
      if(ball.x<ball.r||ball.x>W-ball.r)ball.vx*=-1; if(ball.y<ball.r)ball.vy*=-1;
      if(ball.y>pad.y-ball.r&&ball.y<pad.y+10&&Math.abs(ball.x-pad.x)<pad.w/2){ball.vy=-Math.abs(ball.vy);ball.vx+=(ball.x-pad.x)*0.03;}
      bricks.forEach(function(b){if(b.alive&&ball.x>b.x&&ball.x<b.x+b.w&&ball.y>b.y&&ball.y<b.y+b.h){b.alive=false;ball.vy*=-1;
        score=Math.min(deck.points,score+b.pts);deck.score(score);}});
      if(score>=deck.points){over=true;deck.done();deck.summary('通關!');}
      if(ball.y>H){over=true;deck.done();deck.summary('差一點,得 '+score+' 分,按空白鍵再來');}}
      x.clearRect(0,0,W,H);bricks.forEach(function(b){if(b.alive){x.fillStyle='#77BD1D';x.fillRect(b.x,b.y,b.w,b.h);}});
      x.fillStyle='#fff';x.fillRect(pad.x-pad.w/2,pad.y,pad.w,8);x.beginPath();x.arc(ball.x,ball.y,ball.r,0,7);x.fill();
      x.font='20px sans-serif';x.fillText('分數 '+score+' / '+deck.points+(over?'  (空白鍵重來)':''),12,28);requestAnimationFrame(step);}
    addEventListener('mousemove',function(e){pad.x=e.clientX;});addEventListener('touchmove',function(e){pad.x=e.touches[0].clientX;});
    addEventListener('keydown',function(e){if(e.key==='ArrowLeft')pad.x-=30;if(e.key==='ArrowRight')pad.x+=30;if(e.key===' '&&over)reset();});
    addEventListener('resize',reset);reset();step();
    </script>
  --- widget html end ---
  Step 2, the slide in the deck yaml (title, points, fallback, html = the handle):
    visual:
      kind: widget
      title: 打磚塊 100 分挑戰
      points: 100
      fallback: 打磚塊小遊戲:用滑鼠或左右鍵移動擋板,打掉磚塊累積到 100 分就過關,每個磚塊的分數隨機。
      html: "@w1"
  Narration for such a slide: say the goal and the controls ("用滑鼠或左右鍵移動擋板,打到 100 分就過關"), then let the viewer play; set
  wait: true only when the deck must not go on before they try. The score appears in the player's score chip and in the pack.
  If you are unsure a piece works, make it smaller: a simple correct widget beats an ambitious broken one (there is no way to debug it
  once delivered). Never put secrets or personal data in html.
ai_features: This AI assistant itself: its shipped features, slash commands and built-in skills (built when you ask).
sources:
Material comes from anywhere; you digest it into slides, you do not paste it:
- Files the user uploaded to the chat (file_id): list_uploaded_files, parse_uploaded_file give text (pdf / office / text). A picture the user uploaded is already usable: its handle is "client-file/<file_id>".
- The user's own folders (File Access Points): list_file_access_points, fap_list_files, fap_find_file, fap_read_file read documents and source code. For a whole code base use repo_ask / repo_sql / repo_read_doc (project index). A picture file in a folder is brought in with import_fap_image(ref).
- A website: read the page with the browser tools (browser_get_page_text, browser_screenshot; a screenshot result has a short "client_file_url") and keep the text; a picture whose address is in that text is brought in with import_image_url(url).
- Pictures: every picture seen so far is listed by list_source_images as "@img1", "@img2" ... (tool results are scanned for pictures automatically); use the handle as an image "src". A chart: render_chart.
- SOURCES ARE HINTS, NOT LIMITS. What the user names is where to START; it is never the whole of what you may use. When nothing is named, or a named source has too little, do not stop and do not ask: (1) look in the places above with the topic's keywords; (2) for a subject about THIS AI ("how to use this AI", "what can it do", "all the features") call get_presentation_topic("ai_features"), which lists the real features, slash commands and skills; (3) fill every remaining gap from your own knowledge of the subject, organised into a sensible storyline. Facts you took from a source are stated as such; general knowledge is stated as general explanation. Never invent a figure, a picture or a quote that no tool returned. Always finish with a deck.
- A table in the source -> a table visual (header + rows), NOT a screenshot of a table and NOT bullets, unless it is wider than 8 columns (then pick the columns that matter). A diagram or screenshot in the source -> an image visual with callouts for the parts you explain. Never invent a picture or a number that the source does not contain; if the source lacks something the topic needs, say so in the narration or leave it out.
style:
House style (the deck template, editable in settings): white content slides with a dark title, an accent colour, a dark subtitle bar at the bottom,
dark title/topic slides. The renderer lays everything out; you provide words and structure.
Writing: one idea per slide; the title states the point ("Signature is verified before flashing") not the topic ("Verification");
bullets are fragments of <= 12 words, never the narration repeated word for word; the narration is natural speech, short sentences,
no markdown, no URLs, no emoji; never the user's instructions to you (speaking speed, requested length, tool or field names such as deck.speed / wait: true -- speed goes into deck.speed only); numbers spoken the way they are said. Language: the user's language (deck.lang: zh-TW for Traditional
Chinese, zh-CN, en ...). Keep chapters balanced (3-6 slides each) and finish with a summary slide.
